chapters.chapter: Absolute Zero — the race to the bottom of the temperature scale

videos.title: The Coldest Place on Earth Was a House in Leiden
videos.hook_idea: In December 1877 two men announced three weeks apart that they had liquefied oxygen, and what each of them actually had was a mist that lasted a moment inside a glass tube. Thirty-one years later a professor in Leiden ended a sixteen-hour day holding about sixty cubic centimetres of liquid helium, roughly a teacupful, which nobody in the room could see until a visiting chemist noticed the thermometer appeared to be standing in something. Three years after that his laboratory notebook recorded the resistance of a frozen thread of mercury in three words of Dutch.

lessons.name: A mist that lasted a moment — Cailletet and Pictet's near-simultaneous liquid oxygen, the ironmaster and the professor, cascade machinery and the limits of what could be held
concepts: Louis Paul Cailletet was born at Chatillon-sur-Seine in 1832 and ran his father's ironworks at Chenecieres. He attended the Ecole des Mines in 1854 as an auditeur libre, an unregistered student who simply sat in on the lectures, and never completed the training. At the works he built a cementation box of 350 litres so he could run experiments without waiting on production. His patron Henri Sainte-Claire Deville held Sunday afternoon demonstrations in his laboratory at the Ecole Normale, and it was at one of these, with the Minister of Public Instruction Victor Duruy watching, that Cailletet showed the high-pressure work Deville presented to the Academie des sciences on 22 March 1869. Deville called it a new chemistry, the chemistry of three hundred atmospheres. Victor Regnault had tried to talk him out of attempting the permanent gases at all.

For thirty years the word for oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon monoxide was permanent. Michael Faraday had liquefied chlorine in 1823 and worked through a long list of other gases, and in 1844 he attacked what was left with ether and solid carbon dioxide under vacuum, reaching about minus 110 degrees. The four survivors would not condense at any pressure he could raise, and he called them permanent. Marcelin Berthelot went further and squeezed them above eight hundred atmospheres, and still got nothing. The reason arrived in 1869, when Thomas Andrews in Belfast gave the Bakerian Lecture on the continuity of the gaseous and liquid states and established that every substance has a temperature above which no pressure whatever will liquefy it. For carbon dioxide that temperature is 30.92 degrees. Pressure alone had never been the answer.

Cailletet wrote to Deville on 2 December 1877 to say he had liquefied carbon monoxide and oxygen, and Deville deposited the letter with the Academie the next day as a pli cachete, a sealed note. Cailletet then sat on it. The Academie was holding an election on 17 December to fill a vacancy in its mineralogy section and he was a candidate, so he withheld the announcement rather than let it sway the vote. He was elected corresponding member. Five days later Raoul Pictet succeeded in Geneva, and his telegram reached Paris at eight in the evening on 22 December. Both results were laid before the Academie at the session of 24 December. The sealed note gave Cailletet priority by nineteen days, and Pictet wrote to him directly to say he made no claim on it.

Pictet's telegram of 22 December said that oxygen had been liquefied under 320 atmospheres and 140 degrees of cold by sulphuric and carbonic acids combined, and that the outflow through the tap was continuous and liquid. The sulphuric acid is wrong. What Pictet used was sulphur dioxide, acide sulfureux in French, and somewhere between Geneva and Paris a clerk or a transcriber turned it into acide sulfurique. The error went into the Academie's printed proceedings and historians were still repeating it a century and a third later. His method was a cascade: sulphur dioxide compressed and then boiled off under reduced pressure to reach about minus sixty-five degrees, then carbon dioxide condensed against that to reach about minus a hundred and forty. The oxygen came from potassium chlorate heated inside a wrought-iron retort rated for five hundred atmospheres.

Cailletet's machine worked by letting pressure go. A glass tube of dried gas stood sealed inside a steel cistern, the space around it filled with mercury, and a hydraulic pump forced water in below so the mercury climbed the tube and squeezed the gas. For the oxygen run he pre-cooled it to minus twenty-nine degrees and took it to three hundred atmospheres. Then he opened a valve on the pump. The mercury dropped, the gas expanded against nothing, and by Poisson's formula the temperature should have fallen about two hundred degrees. What appeared in the tube was a thick mist, and then nothing. The historian Faidra Papanelopoulou records, with the hedge that it is said rather than documented, that Cailletet found the expansion trick after an accidental leak. Eugene Ducretet in Paris built a smaller portable version and toured it through Belgium.

A mist proves a gas can condense and gives you nothing else. You cannot measure the boiling point of a fog, or its density, or lower a thermometer into it and leave it there for an hour. Cailletet said as much himself, and wrote that he intended to find the refrigerants that would let him collect the gases properly. Sixteen years later, in December 1893, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes recorded in the fourteenth of his Leiden Communications that he had for the first time collected a quarter of a litre of liquid oxygen in a glass without pressure, and could show it for hours to visitors. He carried a flask of it to the Academy in Amsterdam in May 1894 to show the president of the physical section. What he was announcing was not that oxygen would liquefy, but that it would stand still in a glass.

lessons.name: The first liquid you could keep — Wroblewski and Olszewski at Krakow, immersion in place of spraying, a six-month collaboration and its end
concepts: Zygmunt Florenty Wroblewski was born in Grodno in 1845 and was a student in Kiev when the January Uprising against Russian rule began in 1863. He took part, and was sent to Siberia for six years. He finished his studies afterwards at Heidelberg and took his doctorate at Munich in 1874, then toured the laboratories of London, Oxford, Cambridge and Paris, where he watched Cailletet work at first hand. The Jagiellonian University in Krakow gave him its chair of physics in 1882. Karol Olszewski, born in 1846, had taken his doctorate under Robert Bunsen at Heidelberg in 1872 and had held the Jagiellonian's chair of chemistry since 1876. They began working together at the start of 1883 and sent their first note to Paris only a couple of months later.

Cailletet had cooled his sample tubes by spraying liquid ethylene onto them, a jet that was gone in a moment and cost him the ethylene every time. The Krakow method was to immerse instead. They sealed compressed oxygen in a glass tube and lowered it into a bath of liquid ethylene boiling under reduced pressure, inside a vessel shielded from the surrounding air. Ethylene boils at about minus a hundred and four degrees at ordinary pressure; pumped down to roughly a thirtieth of an atmosphere it holds at about minus a hundred and thirty. The bath stays there for as long as the pump runs. With the oxygen at somewhere between twenty and twenty-seven atmospheres, what formed in the tube was colourless and transparent, with a flat surface and a visible meniscus, boiling quietly.

The day is genuinely uncertain. Two letters from Wroblewski and Olszewski were read at the April 1883 session of the Academy of Learning in Krakow, dating the oxygen to 29 March and the nitrogen to 13 April, and Jagiellonian sources follow those letters. Other Polish accounts give 4 April as the first run they could repeat at will, and some give 5 April. The notes reached the Academie des sciences in Paris later that month. The honest way to put it is that they first saw it in the last days of March and could do it on demand by the first days of April. Their later work, boiling liquid nitrogen under reduced pressure, took them to about minus two hundred and twenty-five degrees, and from that Wroblewski estimated hydrogen's critical temperature at around minus two hundred and thirty-five.

In 1884 the French physicist Jules Jamin published a history of the liquefaction of air in the Revue des Deux Mondes, a literary magazine rather than a scientific journal, and told it in a way that made the Krakow work a derivative of Cailletet's. Wroblewski answered him at thirty pages in the same magazine. He argued that his own research programme had brought him to gas liquefaction independently, that his apparatus carried modifications of his own however much it resembled Cailletet's, that having watched a man work in Paris did not make him that man's pupil, and that the idea of using methane as a refrigerant stronger than ethylene was his. Traces of the argument run through Cailletet's notes to the Academie from 1884 onward. The two men never settled it.

Wroblewski and Olszewski worked together for about six months. After the oxygen, the nitrogen and the carbon monoxide they published separately, and they never collaborated again. Polish accounts give different reasons and give them partisanly: credit for the decisive modification, a physicist and a chemist each unwilling to concede the division of labour, and plain dislike. The reasons are contested in a way the fact of the split is not. What each man had to work with afterwards was small. Nature reported in August 1896 that Olszewski worked with less than seventy cubic centimetres of liquid oxygen at a time and did not have a permanent bath, which meant remaking the cold for every experiment he ran.

In the spring of 1888 Wroblewski was working at night in his laboratory at the Jagiellonian when a paraffin lamp went over and his clothes caught fire. The retellings usually call it a laboratory fire, which overstates it; what the record describes is an overturned lamp and burning clothing. He lived about three weeks. He died in Krakow on 16 April 1888, at forty-two, though at least one published survey gives the eighteenth, and several later retellings date the accident itself to 25 March without any archive behind them. Olszewski went on alone for another twenty-seven years and died in Krakow in 1915. The apparatus and the papers stayed in the city, in the Jagiellonian's museum and its library.

lessons.name: The vessel that made cold keepable — James Dewar's double-walled flask, the Royal Institution plant beneath the lecture room, the decision not to patent and the litigation that followed
concepts: James Dewar held the Jacksonian chair at Cambridge from 1875 and the Fullerian chair of chemistry at the Royal Institution in London from 1877, and he kept both for the rest of his life, living at the Royal Institution. When Johannes van der Waals visited in 1891 he saw the arrangement for himself: Dewar's laboratory, its gas flasks and a hundred-horsepower gas engine sat directly beneath the lecture room where the Friday evening discourses had been given since Faraday's day, and which the Prince of Wales attended. Dewar kept about forty cubic metres of ethylene on the premises. Where Leiden later ran its cascade on a kilogram and a half of ethylene, Dewar's took forty to fifty kilograms, and Nature put his engine at several times the power Leiden needed for the same work.

Dewar introduced a double-walled evacuated vessel at the Royal Institution in 1892. A vacuum flask reduces heat transfer: removing most gas between its walls greatly reduces conduction and circulation through that gas. Silvered surfaces can reduce radiant heat transfer, and a narrow neck limits heat conducted through the solid glass connection. These are features of vacuum-flask design in general; the notes here do not establish that every refinement belonged to the first vessel in 1892. Insulation does not make the liquid cold or stop all heat transfer, but helps it survive longer before boiling away in warmer surroundings. Dewar's liquid hydrogen, obtained six years later, was collected in an insulated vessel.

Dewar did not patent it. He treated the flask as a piece of laboratory equipment and published it. In 1903 Reinhold Burger, a German glassblower who had worked on Dewar's vessels, patented a domestic version, and the name Thermos was chosen by public competition and registered as a trade mark the following year. Dewar went to law to establish his rights and lost, because the invention had been published and was in the public domain. He never earned anything from it. The Dewar papers at the Royal Institution contain, among the lecture notes, a memorandum from 1901 listing the firms then supplying Dewar vacuum vessels, so he was keeping track of the trade four years after giving it away.

On 10 May 1898 at the Royal Institution, Dewar became the first to make liquid hydrogen in a quantity anyone could keep: about twenty cubic centimetres, caught in one of his own vacuum vessels. The method was expansion through a throttle, hydrogen precooled by liquid air and let down in a Linde cycle. Two days later he telegraphed Leiden, liquefied hydrogen and helium. Only the first half was true. His own temperature figures disagreed with each other as well. A platinum resistance thermometer gave him minus two hundred and thirty-eight degrees and a constant-volume hydrogen thermometer gave him minus two hundred and fifty-three, and he published both. The second is right. He demonstrated it at a Friday evening discourse on 20 January 1899, with a newspaper report of the evening pasted into his manuscript notes.

Solid hydrogen came out of a leak. Dewar tried in the autumn of 1898 to freeze liquid hydrogen by pumping on it, got the pressure down to about ten millimetres, and nothing happened. Then a small quantity of air got into the apparatus. Below sixty millimetres, he wrote, the liquid suddenly solidified into a white froth-like mass like frozen foam. His first thought was that he had a sponge of solid air with liquid hydrogen held inside it. What convinced him otherwise was that the white mass evaporated away completely at low pressure and left no substantial solid air behind, and that on letting the pressure rise again it melted at about fifty-five millimetres. He reported it to the British Association at Dover in 1899 and gave no calendar date for it, and none has turned up since.

Helium was a different kind of problem and it had three parts. A cascade works by using each liquefied gas to chill the next, and the chain runs methyl chloride, ethylene, oxygen, air; below that there is no substance to make the next rung from. Oxygen boiled under a few millimetres of pressure reaches about fifty-six degrees above absolute zero, and hydrogen will not condense above thirty-three. Second, helium's own numbers are worse again: it boils at four point two degrees above absolute zero and has no liquid state at all above five point two. Third, letting a gas expand through a throttle only cools it if the gas is already below a temperature particular to that gas, and helium's is about forty-three degrees. Helium had to be got below forty before the throttle would do anything but warm it.

lessons.name: Through measuring to knowing — Kamerlingh Onnes at Leiden, Door meten tot weten, the instrument-makers' school, the cascade plant and the shutdown the city imposed
concepts: The Leiden faculty put two names forward in May 1882 to replace the retiring Pieter Rijke and gave no preference between them: Johannes van der Waals and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes. The letter was signed by the faculty secretary, Hendrik Lorentz, who had been working to get Onnes to Leiden. Onnes was twenty-eight. He gave his inaugural address on Saturday 11 November 1882, printed that year by Brill, and on its sixth page he wrote that Door meten tot weten, through measuring to knowing, was the motto he would wish to write above every physics laboratory. It is usually reported as having been carved over his laboratory door. He said he would wish to write it, standing in a lecture hall. Afterwards there were drinks in the senate chamber, and Lorentz proposed a toast to the other principles Onnes held besides measurement.

He could not buy the instruments he needed, so he trained the people who would make them. From 1885 he took apprentices into the laboratory itself, and in 1901 the arrangement became a school, the Leidse Instrumentmakers School, the only one in the Netherlands. Most of the boys enrolling were sixteen to eighteen. They worked in the laboratory by day, learning to make instruments as part of the ordinary run of the work, and were required to attend evening theory classes at a society called Mathesis Scientiarum Genitrix. Their blue overalls got them the name they are still known by, the blue boys. Onnes went to Schwenningen in Wurttemberg to see the German trade school for instrument-makers and published an account of the visit in 1903, arguing that the Dutch government should support the Leiden school as liberally as Wurttemberg supported its own.

The cascade at Leiden ran in four stages, each one liquefied by the stage above it: methyl chloride down to minus twenty-four degrees, then ethylene, then oxygen at minus a hundred and eighty-three, then air at minus a hundred and ninety-three. The second stage was built entirely of copper, its thin walls ribbed for strength so they would take a vacuum on one side and pressure on the other, and Onnes held the ethylene charge as low as he could because preparing it was such slow work. Alcohol vapour was passed through sulphuric acid and distilled through three connected apparatuses until he could count on gas that was at least ninety-nine per cent ethylene. By 1894 the plant made about fourteen litres of liquid air an hour, and it stayed in use until 1924.

On 12 January 1807 a gunpowder ship blew up on the Rapenburg in the middle of Leiden, killed more than a hundred and fifty people, and left a cleared space the city called the Ruin, which later became Van der Werff Park. The physics laboratory on the Steenschuur stood directly opposite it. In 1896 the municipal executive moved against Onnes under the Nuisance Act over his stores of compressed and liquefiable gases, and recommended putting the cryogenic laboratory out of the city centre altogether. While the case was pending he had to stop the work in dispute, and low-temperature research at Leiden stopped for two years. He argued in his defence that his laboratory burned forty cubic metres of town gas every day and nobody minded that, and that Dewar kept as much ethylene in central London without the slightest opposition.

At the Academy committee's request Onnes wrote to the three other men in the world doing this work and asked them where their laboratories were, what they stored, what precautions they took, and whether the authorities had ever troubled them. Dewar answered from the Royal Institution that a scientific man is certain to do all in his power to avoid accidents and the municipality can have full confidence in him, and offered to come to Leiden himself. Olszewski answered from Krakow that releasing four hundred grams of ethylene had never caused an explosion and nobody there had ever complained. Both letters were printed as appendices to the Academy's report. It partly backfired, because the municipal executive picked out Dewar's phrase about dangers of no ordinary kind and turned it against him. The Hague settled it by paying for safety measures instead, seventeen thousand two hundred guilders in July 1898.

The hydrogen liquefier came into operation in the spring of 1906, in the room Onnes called lab Aa, and it was the fifth cycle in the plant. The compressor took hydrogen to about two hundred atmospheres using a column of mercury to stop the gas slipping past the piston, a design of Cailletet's still at work in Leiden thirty years after Chatillon. Liquid air precooled the hydrogen to about sixty-four degrees above absolute zero before it reached the throttle. The machine made four litres an hour and soon thirteen, where Dewar's made one. The helium itself came from monazite sand shipped from America by way of Hamburg, procured by Onnes's brother Onno, who ran a commercial information office in Amsterdam, and purifying it took four chemists several months.

lessons.name: Sixty millilitres and three words — the helium run of July 1908, a liquid nobody could see, and the mercury result recorded three years later
concepts: Friday 10 July 1908 was wet and windy in Leiden, and it was the twenty-ninth anniversary of the day Onnes took his doctorate at Groningen. He had chosen the date. The Leidsch Dagblad that morning carried the Kaiser's seventieth-birthday greetings to Count Zeppelin, the first herrings of the season delivered to the fish market at Katwijk, and an open-air performance that evening outside a cafe in Oegstgeest, admission twenty-five cents. His wife Betsy woke him before five. A carriage took him from the house on the Galgewater to the laboratory on the Steenschuur, where Gerrit Flim and the technicians had already started. He put his white coat on as he came in. The first job was the hydrogen, and by half past one they had twenty litres of it standing in vacuum vessels.

Cooling of the helium began at half past two, and by three the temperature was down to minus a hundred and eighty. Betsy came in at twenty past four and got a few bites of a sandwich into him. Between half past six and half past seven the helium went round the circuit about twenty times with scarcely anything to be seen but a little swirling, and then at half past seven the thermometer settled on a value that would not move. The chemist Frans Schreinemakers, who had come in to see how it was going, was the one who noticed that the thermometer appeared to be standing in liquid. Onnes lit the vessel from below with an electric lamp. He wrote afterwards that the first appearance of the liquid had really escaped their observation, and that once seen it stood out sharply defined like the edge of a knife against the glass wall.

Liquid helium is nearly impossible to see because it bends light almost exactly as much as its own vapour does. There is no colour in it and barely a meniscus, and the way Onnes finally found the surface was by blowing gas from the valve across it and watching the level go hollow and then rise again. What he had was about sixty cubic centimetres, a teacupful. At half past eight, with ten millilitres left, he began pumping on it to try to freeze it and could not; solid helium took another eighteen years and about twenty-five atmospheres of pressure. At twenty to ten he stopped, sixteen hours after starting. Two of the numbers he published from that night were wrong. He gave helium's boiling point as about four and a half degrees, where it is four point two, and its density about a fifth too high.

The mercury resistor was seven U-shaped glass capillaries in series, each with a small reservoir of mercury so the frozen thread would not break as it cooled, and four platinum feedthroughs carrying thin copper wires out to the measuring gear. Mercury was chosen partly because Leiden could distil it very pure and partly for a practical reason: freezing it inside a capillary gives you a wire without drawing one, so nothing in the drawing can contaminate it. Gilles Holst suggested solidifying it with liquid nitrogen. The cryostat was new that April, and the purpose of 8 April 1911 was to test whether liquid helium could be transferred into it at all. The resistors were installed in case the transfer worked. Flim's team started at seven in the morning and Onnes came in at twenty past eleven.

Just after noon the gas thermometer read five degrees above absolute zero. Through the afternoon they established that liquid helium does not conduct electricity, measured its dielectric constant, and Holst measured the resistance of the mercury and of a gold wire at four point three degrees. Then they pumped the vapour pressure down to about three degrees and at exactly four o'clock, says the notebook, measured both again. Onnes wrote three words, Kwik nagenoeg nul, mercury practically zero, and under them that he had repeated it with gold. The entry is at three degrees, not at four point two, and nobody in the room saw a sharp transition that day. Later the same afternoon they wrote that just before the lowest temperature the boiling suddenly stopped and was replaced by evaporation in which the liquid visibly shrank.

That second entry is liquid helium going superfluid at two point one seven degrees, and it took twenty-seven years for anyone to explain it. Both observations sat unread for most of a century, and the reason is a slip of the pencil. Onnes dated his notes by day and month, and for 8 April he left the year off; in an unrelated experiment run that May with a visitor from Lausanne he wrote 1910 when he meant 1911, because he and the same visitor had run a similar series the year before. Dirk van Delft and Peter Kes, reading notebooks fifty-six and fifty-seven at the Boerhaave museum in Leiden, published what was in them in 2010. It also disposed of the story that a sleepy apprentice in blue overalls let the helium boil away and revealed the effect by accident.

lessons.name: What zero resistance allows — explanatory background
concepts: In an ideal closed superconducting loop, an electric current can persist after the external electrical power supply that established it is disconnected. This follows from the absence of electrical resistance; ordinary resistive decay in an isolated inductive loop obeys L dI/dt + R I = 0, so the R=0 model has constant current. This is explanatory physical context for superconductivity, not a claim that the 1911 mercury measurement itself was a long-duration persistent-current experiment. The loop must remain superconducting, within its temperature, current and field limits. Not every metal becomes superconducting. Cooling can require energy, and extracting power changes the system: this is not free energy. No measured duration is supplied by this note; do not invent a years-long historical demonstration.

chapters.chapter: Nuclear Fission — the discovery that was made in two countries at once

videos.title: The Letter That Split the Atom
videos.hook_idea: Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn worked together in Berlin for thirty-one years, the first five of them in a basement room that had been a woodworking shop, which she was forbidden to leave and which had no lavatory she was allowed to use. In July 1938 she crossed into the Netherlands with ten marks in her purse and a diamond ring Hahn had given her to bribe a guard with. Five months later he wrote to her at eleven at night to say their radium was behaving like barium, and asked her to find a way out of it. She and her nephew worked it out on a walk in the snow. The paper that first used the word fission carries her name. The Nobel Prize for the discovery does not.

lessons.name: The carpentry shop — Meitner's arrival in Berlin, Fischer's exclusion of women, the basement room and the conditions attached to it, and the years without pay
concepts: Lise Meitner was born in Vienna in November 1878, the third of eight children of Philipp Meitner, one of the first Jewish lawyers admitted to practise in Austria and a chess master of some standing. Her leaving certificate from the Madchen-Burgerschule is dated 15 July 1892, when she was thirteen. It records bookkeeping arithmetic but no algebra, some geography and science, drawing, singing, feminine handwork and a little French. Her behaviour was rated entirely appropriate and her diligence only satisfactory. Austrian universities were closed to women until 1897, so she prepared for the school-leaving examination privately, passed it in 1901, and took her doctorate in physics at Vienna in 1906, the second woman there to do so. Her birth is recorded on two different days, the seventh of November and the seventeenth, and she used the earlier one all her life.

Women could not enrol at Prussian universities, so Meitner had to ask Max Planck's personal permission to attend his lectures. He received her kindly and invited her to his home, and there he said to her, but you are a doctor already, what more do you want. When she answered that she would like to gain some real understanding of physics, he said a few friendly words and did not pursue it. Eleven years before that, a Berlin journalist named Arthur Kirchhoff had surveyed about a hundred academics on higher education for women. Planck, then thirty-nine and the father of four, had written that he would admit a gifted woman on a trial basis and always revocably, but that Amazons are abnormal even in intellectual fields, and that nature itself has designated for woman her vocation as mother and housewife.

Emil Fischer, the organic chemist who ran the Chemical Institute, kept women out of it altogether. The reason he gave was that he was afraid they would set their hair on fire, having once had a student with an exotic hairstyle. What he allowed instead was a basement room that had been a woodworking shop, which Otto Hahn had already fitted out with electroscopes for measuring radiation. Meitner could work there and nowhere else, not even in the laboratory upstairs where Hahn did his chemistry. The concession was possible only because the shop had a separate entrance from the street, so she never had to pass through the institute at all. There was no lavatory in the building she was permitted to use, so she walked to a restaurant down the road.

The shop was bad for the work as well as for her dignity. Radioactive liquids were spilled on the benches, radioactive gases vented into the room, decayed, and settled as dust, and the background from all of it made weak activities impossible to measure. Hahn could not do proper chemistry there either, and Alfred Stock, who ran inorganic chemistry, quietly let him use a corner of one of his private laboratories. When Prussia admitted women to its universities in the summer of 1908, Fischer lifted every restriction at once, welcomed women in, and had a ladies' room installed. Several of his assistants resented it. When one of them came across Meitner and Hahn together, he would say only, good day, Herr Hahn.

Neither of them was paid. Hahn lived on an allowance from his father and Meitner on an allowance from hers, though hers was the smaller, and her father died in 1910. Her first salary came late in 1912, when Planck made her his assistant at the Institute for Theoretical Physics and set her to grading his students' papers. Assistant was the lowest rung on the academic ladder, and she was the first woman to hold such a post in Prussia. She always called it the turning point of her early career. Why Planck did it is not written down anywhere. With her father two years dead, he may simply have been afraid that money would force her back to Vienna.

The Kaiser Wilhelm Institutes opened on a cold wet day, 23 October 1912, and officials presented Meitner to the Kaiser. The new institute was privately funded and had no rule against women, though she worked there at first as an unpaid guest in Hahn's section. They took four rooms in the north wing of the ground floor and invented a contamination routine as they went. The strongest preparations were left behind in the old contaminated wood shop. Chemistry and measurement were done in separate rooms. A roll of toilet paper hung beside every telephone and every door handle so that nothing was touched with a bare hand, people sat only on chairs marked yellow, and nobody shook hands in greeting. Meitner was the strictest of them, and twenty-five years later her rooms were still clean enough to measure very weak activities in.

lessons.name: Twenty-one years of her own section — the 1917 split of the laboratory, protactinium and the medal, Fermi's neutron papers and the collaboration she began
concepts: In July 1915 Meitner went to Vienna and volunteered as an X-ray nurse with the Austrian army. She was accepted, trained and vaccinated within days and sent to a military hospital at Lemberg in Galicia, about forty kilometres from the Russian front. She left Vienna on 4 August with two hundred and twenty men, fifty nurses and ten physicians, and spent sixty hours on the train. She wrote to her friend Elisabeth Schiemann that she had never expected it to be as awful as it was, that one could hear their screams and groans as well as see their horrible wounds. By 18 October she had done over two hundred X-rays. She wrote to Hahn that at night when she could not sleep she felt slightly homesick for physics, but that during the day she thought only of the patients.

There had to be something long-lived decaying into actinium, and nobody had found it. Meitner and Hahn went looking before the war and failed, and she came back to it in 1917 with a silica residue that had been separated out of pitchblende early in 1914. Hahn was in the army. She did nearly all of it alone, on one and a half grams of silica, in the first turnip winter, with no students, no technicians, almost no fuel and no fresh pitchblende to be had. The paper went to Physikalische Zeitschrift on 16 March 1918 and proposed the name protactinium. Hahn was listed as the senior author. Frederick Soddy and John Cranston in Scotland reported the same substance that June, neither side knowing of the other, and accepted the Berlin name.

In 1919 the Association of German Chemists gave Hahn its Emil Fischer Medal for his radiochemistry, protactinium included. It then voted separately to present Meitner with a copy of Hahn's medal. Hahn was disturbed by this. Meitner was not, and wrote to him that she found it very gratifying and very justified that he should receive it, that it seemed to her less justified that she should also come away with something, and that of course he must go. That same year she was given the title of professor, in all likelihood the first woman in Prussia to hold it, and came home to find flowers in her apartment and more flowers in the laboratory. When she gave her first lecture as a university lecturer in 1922, on the significance of radioactivity for cosmic processes, a press wrote asking permission to publish her lecture on the significance of radioactivity for cosmetic processes. She enjoyed the misprint for years.

Fermi's group in Rome posted preprints to about forty of the most active nuclear physicists in 1934, which is how Meitner learned that neutrons could make new radioactivity. On 16 May she wrote to Fermi asking him to send his articles once more, because she had misplaced the ones he had kindly sent and could not find them again. She found the uranium results interesting enough that she went to Hahn and proposed resuming their direct collaboration. Hahn told it differently for the rest of his life, dating the start to an American note in Physical Review that could not have reached Germany until weeks after she first approached him. Their own first joint paper says that they had now undertaken a thorough investigation of these uranium processes, and cites two earlier neutron studies of hers.

In 1934 the German chemist Ida Noddack published a note in Angewandte Chemie attacking Fermi's reasoning. He had shown only that his new substance was none of the elements just below uranium, she wrote, and had not excluded the ones far down the table. It is conceivable, she wrote, that in the bombardment of heavy nuclei with neutrons, these nuclei break up into several large fragments. Nobody took it up, and the reasons are not only the obvious one. She offered no mechanism, no calculation and no experiment; everything then known about nuclear change involved one or a few units of charge at a time; and her own claim to have found element forty-three was disputed and had twice spilled into print. Meitner did not take it up either. No one really thought of fission before its discovery, she wrote in 1963.

The neutron sources were powdered beryllium mixed with about a hundred milligrams of radium sulphate and melted airtight into small glass tubes, and the institute had six of them. To slow the neutrons down, the uranium and the sources went together into a closed paraffin block drilled with bore-holes. Ten to a hundred grams of uranium had to be irradiated to get anything measurable, and what it produced weighed less than a millionth of a millionth of a gram, far below what any balance or spectrograph of the day could find. Only the radiation gave it away. The counter tubes were made in the institute's own workshop out of aluminium turned down on a lathe to a tenth of a millimetre, so the wall would not absorb the radiation on its way in. Their great mistake, Meitner said later, was to examine only what precipitated and never the filtrate.

lessons.name: Ten marks and a diamond ring — the Anschluss and her change of status, the ban on academic travel, and the crossing into the Netherlands
concepts: Meitner was Jewish by descent and had been baptised a Lutheran in 1908, and under the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 that made her Jewish. She had lost her university teaching licence in 1933. What kept her working was a double accident: she was an Austrian citizen, and the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute was privately funded rather than a state body, so the civil service racial laws did not reach her. On 12 March 1938 Austria ceased to exist and its citizens became Germans. Both protections went in a single day and her passport became invalid. Then the other half of the trap closed. On 4 July she wrote in her diary that academics would no longer be granted permission to travel abroad. She was in a country that would not let her work and would not let her leave.

Niels Bohr had come to Berlin that June, seen how things stood, and gone home to look for a position for her. He asked Hans Kramers to try the Netherlands, and Kramers went to Dirk Coster at Groningen, who had been her friend since 1921. Adriaan Fokker did the paperwork, petitioning the Dutch ministers of justice and of education on 28 June and appealing to Dutch industrialists, Philips among them. Because foreigners could not work for pay in the Netherlands, de Haas and van Arkel arranged an unpaid lectureship at Leiden as the legal fiction that would let her in. Peter Debye, running the physics institute in Berlin, carried the messages. And a friend of Coster's named Ebels, a local politician from the border region, went and spoke to the guards.

On 12 July she came in to the institute early and Hahn told her the plan. To avoid drawing attention she kept her ordinary routine and stayed until eight in the evening, correcting a colleague's paper for publication. Hahn and Paul Rosbaud helped her pack, two small suitcases by most accounts and one by the Coster family's, with only summer clothes in them so that if she were stopped she could say she was going on holiday. Hahn gave her a diamond ring he had inherited from his mother, to sell or to bribe with. She spent that night at his house. In the morning she met Coster at the railway station and the two of them pretended to have run into each other by chance. She had ten marks in her purse and she was fifty-nine years old.

They took a lightly used branch line to the frontier at Bad Nieuweschans and crossed without incident. The Dutch side had been prepared: written provisional admission had come through the day before, the head of the border guards had been spoken to, and Ebels had spoken to the guards themselves. The German side had not been prepared at all, and that was the whole of the danger. She was a German Jew without valid papers leaving a state that had just forbidden academics to travel, and Coster was risking arrest standing beside her. Miep Coster's recollection in the family was that the German guards let her through because they took Frau Professor for a professor's wife. Her diary for 13 July records the crossing and no drama. From the German side nothing survives at all.

The pension was a charade. She applied to retire from the Kaiser Wilhelm Society on 23 August 1938, the agreements were not honoured, and the money never came. Carl Bosch tried to have her belongings shipped to Sweden and the Reich Ministry of Education insisted they stay in Germany. Richard Willstatter, leaving the same year, got his papers only after signing over his house and everything in it including his books, and crossed into Switzerland having paid an export duty on his suit, his soap and his toothbrush. Hahn told the institute that Meitner had gone to Vienna to see relatives, and a few days later it closed for the summer. She flew to Copenhagen on 28 July and reached Sweden on the first of August.

Manne Siegbahn had won the physics prize in 1924 and ran the new Nobel Institute for Physics in Stockholm. Meitner found out only after she arrived that he had not wanted her. The money that paid her came from the Nobel Foundation, obtained by Carl Oseen at Eva von Bahr-Bergius's request rather than from Siegbahn, and nobody had thought about the fact that she could not work without help. She wrote to Hahn in February 1939 that in Dahlem, if she needed something made, she talked it over with Gille, who did the mechanical work and the drawings, and that here she was told every time to please make a drawing. In another letter she wrote: if only you could see my daily work. I have absolutely no help. I put counters together, evacuate them, test them for leaks.

lessons.name: Our radium acts like barium — the four failed separations, Hahn's letter of 19 December, and the journey to Kungalv
concepts: Radium is only ever found in the company of barium, its chemical near-twin, and the way to part them is fractional crystallisation, the method Marie Curie had proved out on radium between 1899 and 1902. Radium comes out preferentially with the first crystals, so the head fraction should be measurably richer than the ones after it. On 25 November Hahn and Strassmann irradiated eleven grams of ammonium diuranate for sixteen hours, dissolved it in hydrochloric acid, added a gram and a half of barium chloride to carry the radium, and crystallised it out in three fractions. They counted equal amounts of each, three hundred and fifty milligrams at a time, through the same counter tube. The activity fell steadily as the substance decayed, exactly as it should. But there was no jump between the fractions. Nothing had enriched.

They ran it again on 28 November as the bromide, and on 8 December against the longest-lived one, and got the same answer both times. Suspecting the amounts were simply too small for the method to bite, they spiked ordinary barium with genuine natural radium and fractionated that, and it behaved perfectly. So the method was sound. On the evening of 16 December they combined the two experiments into one. Fifteen and a half grams of uranium irradiated overnight, the irradiation stopped at eight in the morning, two and a half hours allowed for the short-lived substance to decay, and then the artificial radium mixed with a known genuine radium isotope and fractionated together with two grams of barium, in the same solution, in the same glassware, at the same moment. The genuine radium enriched. The artificial one did not.

Hahn wrote to her at eleven at night on Monday 19 December, from the laboratory, waiting for Strassmann to come back at a quarter to twelve so that he could go home. There is something about the radium isotopes, he wrote, that is so remarkable that for now we are telling only you. The half-lives were exact, they could be separated from every element except barium, every reaction fitted, and only one thing did not: the fractionation does not work, our radium isotopes act like barium. He asked her to find a way out of it, and wrote that if she could suggest anything it would still be like a result of the three of us. She answered on the twenty-first that the assumption of such a thoroughgoing breakup seemed very difficult to her, but that in nuclear physics we have experienced so many surprises that one cannot unconditionally say it is impossible.

She left Stockholm on 23 December for Kungalv on the west coast, to spend the holidays with Eva von Bahr-Bergius. Frisch came up from Copenhagen; he had always spent Christmas with her in Berlin. Hahn had posted the manuscript to her Stockholm address and she would not see it for a week, so all she had was the letter. Frisch's account, written about forty years afterwards, is the only one there is. He came out of his room on the first morning and found her studying it, wanted to talk about an experiment of his own, and was told he had to read that letter first. He suggested the chemists might have made a mistake and she waved it away; Hahn was too good a chemist for that. Then they went out into the snow, Frisch on skis and Meitner on foot, and she proved she could keep up.

Frisch later recalled that he and Meitner sat on a tree trunk and worked through the explanation on scraps of paper. They used a liquid-drop model: nuclear binding tends to hold the nucleus together, while the positive charges repel one another. A disturbed heavy nucleus can deform and divide into large fragments, which need not be equal halves. Frisch estimated that the charged fragments would move apart with about two hundred million electron volts of energy. Meitner used known nuclear masses to estimate a corresponding mass difference of roughly a fifth of a proton's mass. Mass-energy accounting compares the complete incoming system, including a neutron absorbed by uranium, with all the outgoing products; it does not mean a proton disappears. Their approximate estimates agreed, making the proposed division physically plausible. The outdoor scene is Frisch's later recollection, not a contemporaneous record of every step.

Hahn had been groping toward the same thing and got the arithmetic wrong. On 28 December he wrote asking whether uranium might break into a barium and a masurium, since a barium of 138 and a masurium of 101 make 239. He was balancing the weights and not the charges, and he admitted as much in the same letter: of course the atomic numbers don't add up. The guess went into the page proofs, so it appeared in print, and readers including Einstein concluded that the Berlin chemists did not understand their own result. It is also the reason nobody in Berlin looked for krypton, which is what barium's partner has to be. Frisch told Bohr on 3 January and the conversation lasted five minutes, because Bohr agreed at once and could not imagine why he had not thought of it himself.

lessons.name: A physicist who never lost her humanity — the naming of fission, the Nobel Prize awarded to Hahn alone, the forty-nine nominations, and the later review of the committee's records
concepts: Frisch needed a word for it. He went to William Arnold, an American biologist on a fellowship at Bohr's institute, and asked what you call the process in which one bacterium divides into two. Binary fission, Arnold said. Frisch asked whether he could use fission on its own, and Arnold said he could. On Friday the thirteenth of January, Frisch did the experiment Meitner had proposed to him by telephone from Stockholm: put uranium beside an ionisation chamber, set the amplifier so that only very large pulses would register at all, and watch the screen. At first there was nothing but the small pulses of the uranium's own alpha particles. Then Arnold picked up a neutron source by its handle and held it next to the sample, and huge spikes appeared.

Hahn and Strassmann's chemistry paper was submitted to Naturwissenschaften on 22 December 1938 and appeared on 6 January 1939. Meitner was not one of its authors. Absence from the author list must not be expanded into a claim that her name appeared nowhere in the paper, or attributed to a specific publication prohibition without evidence. The paper concludes that as chemists they ought to replace radium with barium, while they still find the implied change difficult to reconcile with familiar nuclear physics. Meitner and Frisch posted their interpretation to Nature on 16 January and it came out on 11 February, under the title Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction. It introduced the term fission in print. Chemical identification and physical interpretation were complementary contributions by different author pairs.

The 1944 chemistry prize was decided in November 1945 and announced on the fifteenth, and Hahn could not be told, because he was interned at Farm Hall in England and his whereabouts were secret. He read it in the Daily Telegraph. His nine fellow prisoners celebrated on the eighteenth with speeches and songs they wrote for the occasion. He was still not allowed to travel that December, so the chairman of the chemistry committee announced at the ceremony that the decision of the academy could not at present be implemented by the awarding of the prize. King Gustav handed it over a year later, on 10 December 1946, for his discovery of the fission of heavy atomic nuclei. Meitner and Strassmann were not included. Meitner said Hahn fully deserved it and that there was really no doubt about it.

Nobel records stay sealed for fifty years. When the 1944 chemistry and 1946 physics deliberations came open in the middle of the nineties, Elisabeth Crawford, Ruth Lewin Sime and Mark Walker went through them and published what they found in Nature in 1996 and in Physics Today the year after. Four things had gone wrong. The committees were built to judge chemistry or physics and this was both; they had little expertise in theoretical physics; wartime Sweden was cut off, so the members relied on their own reading; and nobody allowed for the way German persecution had bent the published record, in which Meitner's name had simply stopped appearing. The report on her work was written by a member of Siegbahn's own school, who argued that the physics prize was given for experimental rather than theoretical work.

In 1943 she was invited to join the British group going to Los Alamos, Frisch among them. It would have meant good physics, people she knew, and a way out of Sweden. She refused immediately and there was no discussion about it. She had been at Lemberg in 1915 and she had heard what she heard. Among scientists anywhere in that war, almost nobody refused outright. Ten years later she wrote to Hahn about something else that had been eating at her. A Max Planck Society report had called her the longtime Mitarbeiterin, the assistant, of its president, and Heisenberg had used the same word about her in print. In 1917, she wrote, she had been entrusted with creating the physics section and had led it for twenty-one years. Try for once to imagine yourself in my place, she asked him. He never answered.

She moved to Cambridge in 1960 to be near Frisch, and at eighty-five she kept a small notebook with a section headed Questions for O.R., which held entries like nuclear form factor and spin-spin relaxation alongside highfalutin and juke box. Hahn died on 28 July 1968 and Frisch did not tell her, thinking she was too frail to be told. She died in her sleep just after midnight on 27 October 1968, a few days short of ninety, not knowing. She is buried in the churchyard at Bramley in Hampshire, beside her brother Walter. Only the family came, there were no eulogies, and the organist played Bach. Frisch chose the stone and wrote the words cut into it: Lise Meitner, a physicist who never lost her humanity. In 1982 a team at Darmstadt made a single atom of element 109 and named it meitnerium.

lessons.name: Present-day significance of nuclear fission (background context)
concepts: Nuclear fission releases energy when a heavy nucleus splits; emitted neutrons can initiate further fissions in a chain reaction. In nuclear power reactors, fission of uranium or plutonium releases heat that turns water into steam and drives a turbine to generate electricity. This provides present-day context for the significance of discovering fission, without claiming that the 1938 discovery alone supplied a working reactor. Source: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy, Fission and Fusion: What is the Difference?, April 1, 2021, https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/fission-and-fusion-what-difference (retrieved 2026-09-24; cached at artifacts/youtube-hooks-20260924/prompt-reevaluation/context-evidence/doe-fission.html).

chapters.chapter: The Einstein-Bohr Argument — and the hardware that finally settled it

videos.title: Ten Sheets of Glass in a Berkeley Basement
videos.hook_idea: In August 1935 Einstein wrote to Schrodinger about a keg of gunpowder which, after a year, quantum mechanics would have to describe as a blend of not-yet and already-exploded. Schrodinger wrote back a month later with a cat. For the next thirty years the disagreement was filed under philosophy rather than physics, and when a man at CERN finally turned it into a question with a measurable answer, his paper drew two citations in five years from anyone other than himself. It was settled in a sub-basement in Berkeley, with twenty sheets of window glass, a brass gear of the kind used in film projectors, and two hundred hours of counting photons that arrived at a rate of two every ten seconds.

lessons.name: Twenty-nine people at the Hotel Britannique — the fifth Solvay conference, what the printed proceedings record, and what survives only as recollection
concepts: The fifth Solvay conference met in Brussels from the twenty-fourth to the twenty-ninth of October 1927, on the subject of electrons and photons. Twenty-nine people attended. Seventeen of them either held a Nobel Prize already or would be given one later, and in the group photograph taken by Benjamin Couprie for the Solvay institute, Einstein sits dead centre of the front row and Bohr stands at the right-hand end of the middle one. Something else survives from that week that almost nobody has seen. Irving Langmuir, a chemist who was there as a participant, shot about two minutes of home movie during an intermission, and twenty-one of the twenty-nine walk past his camera. It is the only moving picture of the meeting that exists.

The printed proceedings do record Einstein in the general discussion, and what he said there is concrete. Consider a single particle sent at a screen. The wave that describes it spreads out and arrives everywhere on the screen at once, but the particle itself is only ever found at one spot. The interpretation that treats the wave as the probability of finding the particle at a given point, he said, assumes an entirely peculiar mechanism of action at a distance, which prevents the wave from producing an effect in two places. His proposed remedy was equally plain: do not describe the process by the wave alone, but also say where the particle actually is while it is travelling. That is the whole of his objection, stated in a room, in October 1927.

The thing everybody quotes is not in the proceedings at all. The delegates were staying at the Grand Hotel Britannique, and the story that comes down is of Einstein arriving at breakfast with a new thought experiment, Pauli and Heisenberg waving it away, Bohr taking it seriously all day, and the whole company reassembling at dinner with Bohr's answer ready. The trouble is that the man who told it, Otto Stern, was not one of the twenty-nine, and may have been describing some other gathering. What Bohr himself wrote, twenty-two years afterwards, is only that Einstein's attitude gave rise to ardent discussions within a small circle. He does record the dice, though, in German: Einstein mockingly asked whether the providential authorities really took recourse to dice-playing.

Paul Ehrenfest of Leiden was the close friend of both men and in effect the referee; Einstein and Bohr each stayed in his house when they visited. Bohr's account has him at the peak of the argument teasing Einstein about the resemblance between his position and that of the people who had refused to accept relativity, and then adding at once that he would find no relief in his own mind until agreement with Einstein was reached. The sharper version that circulates, in which Ehrenfest says he is ashamed of him, is somebody's later reconstruction; Bohr gives the sense but not the words. Ehrenfest had written to his students that every new issue of the journals immersed him in blind panic and that he knew absolutely nothing. He killed his disabled son and then himself in Amsterdam in September 1933.

Three years later, at the next Solvay conference, Einstein brought a machine. A box with a hole in its side, the hole opened and closed by a shutter worked by a clock inside it. Fill the box with radiation, set the clock to open the shutter for a very short interval, and one photon leaves at a moment you know as precisely as you please. Weigh the box before and weigh it after, and because weight is energy, you know the photon's energy as precisely as you please too. Both at once, which quantum mechanics says you cannot have. Bohr's answer was to draw it. He sketched the box in section so that you could see the clockwork inside, hanging from a spring balance, with a pointer reading against a scale fixed to the support.

The drawing is the argument. To read that pointer precisely you must let the box settle, and the longer the weighing takes the more it costs you elsewhere. But the box also rises or sinks a little in the earth's gravity while you weigh it, and a clock that moves in a gravitational field runs at a different rate. Bohr had beaten Einstein with Einstein's own result, the one that shifts the lines in the sun's spectrum. Leon Rosenfeld, who was there, described Bohr spending the whole evening in agitation, going from one scientist to another, unable to find a way out, and the pair of them leaving the club with Einstein walking tranquilly and Bohr trotting along beside him. Bohr's own account says nothing of the kind, and gives Einstein credit for helping to resolve it.

lessons.name: Smothered by formalism — the EPR paper at Princeton, the newspaper that ran ahead of the journal, Einstein's objection to the drafting, and the letter to Schrodinger
concepts: The idea came out of a teatime conversation at the Institute for Advanced Study between Einstein and his two research associates, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen. The paper is called Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete, and it is four pages long. Podolsky submitted it to Physical Review on 25 March 1935, and by the institute's own account it was sent out for publication the day after it arrived. It appeared on 15 May. Its last sentence says the authors are forced to conclude that the description given by wave functions is not complete, and a page earlier it says plainly that they believe a complete theory is possible. Five days before submitting it, Einstein had written a letter of reference for Podolsky, who was about to leave for Cincinnati.

On 4 May, eleven days before the journal appeared, the New York Times ran the story on page eleven under the headline Einstein Attacks Quantum Theory, with the subhead Scientist and Two Colleagues Find It Is Not Complete Even Though Correct. The piece is datelined Princeton, the third of May, and it says in its own words that the result had been learned exclusively by Science Service, a news syndicate in Washington. So the leak did not come from the paper's own reporting. It prints the article's exact title and quotes from the text. Einstein was incensed, and the Times subsequently carried a statement from him objecting to the practice of announcing scientific results in newspapers.

He was not much happier with the paper itself. Podolsky had been given the job of composing it after several discussions, and by every account Einstein never checked the draft before it went. He wrote to Schrodinger on 19 June that for reasons of language this had been written by Podolsky after several discussions, that it had not come out as well as he had originally wanted, and that the essential thing had been, so to speak, smothered. The German word he used means erudition or learnedness, and translators have rendered it as formalism, as erudition, and as buried by learning. What he cared about was whether two things a long way apart can be separate things at all. What Podolsky had written was a paper about quantities that cannot be measured together.

Bohr answered twice. A short letter to Nature on 13 July, holding the ground and announcing that a full reply was coming, and then the reply itself, received the same day and published on 15 October, exactly five months after the original. He gave it the identical title, word for word, with one definite article inserted, which is still the quickest way to tell the two papers apart on a shelf. His central move was to deny that anything mechanical was happening at all: in this situation, he wrote, there is no question of a mechanical disturbance of the system under investigation. Rosenfeld later put the argument more clearly than Bohr ever managed. The measurement on the first particle does not disturb the second. It decides what you are able to predict about it.

That August, Einstein wrote to Schrodinger with what he called a crude macroscopic example. A substance in chemically unstable equilibrium, a charge of gunpowder that can combust of its own accord, with an average life of a year. At the start the wave function describes a reasonably well-defined state. After a year it describes a sort of blend of not-yet and already-exploded systems, and no art of interpretation can turn that into a description of a real state of affairs, because in reality there is nothing in between exploded and not exploded. Schrodinger replied in September that he had built an example very similar to the exploding powder keg, and set out the cat. He shortened the clock from a year to an hour and added an atom, a counter, a relay, a hammer, and a flask of acid.

The cat is one paragraph, at the end of the first of three weekly instalments in Naturwissenschaften that autumn. The English word for the thing that actually interested him came out of the same year's work in another journal: Schrodinger wrote a paper for the Cambridge Philosophical Society in 1935 and used entanglement there, having used the German Verschrankung in the German one. He coined it twice in a year, in two languages. Arthur Fine, who edited the correspondence, found that he had worked the whole idea out in his letters to Einstein before any of it reached print. His own compressed statement of it is the best anybody has managed: the best possible knowledge of a whole does not necessarily include the best possible knowledge of all its parts.

lessons.name: A hobby, and a paper nobody read — Bell's paid work at CERN, the 1964 paper written on leave, the journal that folded, and the years of near-total neglect
concepts: He was born in Belfast in July 1928 and called Stewart at home, after his mother's family; he became John at university. Of the four children he was the only one who stayed at school past fourteen, and he went to the technical high school because the family could not afford the prestigious ones. At sixteen he was a year under the age for entry to Queen's University, so he took a job as a technician in the physics teaching laboratory there, and the lecturing staff lent him books and let him sit in on the first-year lectures. He entered as a student the following year on his technician's savings. He graduated twice, with first-class honours in experimental physics in 1948 and in mathematical physics in 1949. A bad crash on a motorbike cut him around the mouth, which is why he grew the beard.

His paid work was accelerators and particle physics, and he was good at it. He published about eighty papers in the field between 1955 and 1984, he helped analyse the first neutrino experiments at CERN in 1963, and for most of his life his most-cited paper was not the famous one but a 1969 piece with Roman Jackiw explaining why a particle that theory said could not decay did so anyway. Their answer required that the charges of the elementary particles sum to zero, which is part of how we know quarks come in three kinds. Quantum theory was the hobby. In 1953 Rudolf Peierls asked him to give a short talk at Birmingham, and Bell offered a choice of accelerator design or the foundations of quantum theory. Peierls picked accelerators. Bell waited another decade.

The leave came in 1963: a year at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, then Brandeis, then Wisconsin. The paper's own byline says on leave of absence from SLAC and CERN, and it acknowledges that the first draft was written at Brandeis. It runs to six pages, titled On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen paradox with no punctuation at all between the three names, and it went into a journal called Physics, printed on the masthead in English, French and Russian. Two physicists at Bell Laboratories had founded it to carry only papers worth every physicist's attention, and they read every submission themselves. It charged authors nothing and paid them ten cents a word, which was the reverse of American practice. It published fewer than a hundred articles in four volumes and stopped in 1968.

Nobody read it. By 2005 the paper had been cited more than two thousand times, but only a hundred and forty-four of those came before 1982. In the five years before John Clauser got hold of it, exactly three papers cited it: one by Bell himself; one by Clark and Turner, who noticed the conflict it predicted but exploited neither the conflict nor any way of testing it; and one by Sachs, which mentions it in passing. The average physics paper of that period drew seven to nine citations. In July 1969 a colloquium called Quantum Theory and Beyond met at Cambridge, organised by David Bohm and chaired by Otto Frisch, attended by very nearly every person alive who should have cared. Not one of them cited Bell.

There is a second paper, and it was written first. Bell wrote it at Stanford in 1964, taking apart the proof by von Neumann that had been used for thirty years to rule hidden variables out entirely. It did not appear until 1966, because the journal mislaid his revised version, and by the time the editor wrote asking about the revisions Bell had gone back to CERN and the letter was not forwarded. Two years lost to a misfiled manuscript and an unforwarded letter. The consequence is visible on the page: the 1966 paper cites the 1964 one, and the 1964 one carries an entry in its reference list reading J. S. Bell, to be published, pointing forward at a paper that was already finished. He wrote in it that the paradox is resolved in the way which Einstein would have liked least.

The first serious reaction Bell got arrived five years after publication, in a letter from an American graduate student, and he answered it on 5 March 1969. In view of the general success of quantum mechanics, he wrote, it is very hard for me to doubt the outcome of such experiments. However, I would prefer these experiments, in which the crucial concepts are very directly tested, to have been done and the results on record. Moreover, there is always the slim chance of an unexpected result, which would shake the world. He guessed wrong about where it would happen, expecting the decisive work to come from particle physics. Asked years later where he had stood before he proved Einstein wrong, he said Einstein's intellectual superiority over Bohr had seemed to him enormous.

lessons.name: A room in the sub-basement of Birge Hall — Clauser and Freedman's borrowed apparatus, the absence of funding and of support, and the result he did not want
concepts: John Francis Clauser was born in Pasadena at the end of 1942. His father was an aeronautical engineer who had worked with Theodore von Karman on the physics of fluids, and who told his son that the mathematics of flowing fluid and the mathematics of quantum mechanics looked very alike, that he did not understand quantum mechanics, and that he had rather pre-programmed the boy as the one who might solve the problem he could not. His other piece of advice was to look at the data, because people will have lots of fancy theories, but you should always go back to the original data. Clauser's doctorate at Columbia was on the cosmic microwave background, which is to say on measuring extremely faint signals, and that is the training that mattered. He wanted, in his own words, to shake the world.

Abner Shimony had a doctorate in philosophy from Yale and a second one in physics from Princeton under Eugene Wigner, and in 1968 he set a graduate student named Michael Horne to design a version of the experiment that could actually be built. Early the next year Shimony saw Clauser's abstract in the bulletin of the American Physical Society and told Horne they had been scooped. He telephoned Clauser and proposed they join forces. The paper the four of them wrote, with Richard Holt at Harvard, came out in October 1969 and did three things. It rewrote Bell's theorem for real equipment. It showed that none of the existing data could settle anything. And it pointed at an experiment Carl Kocher had already run in 1967 with the right apparatus at the wrong angles, zero and ninety degrees, where the two predictions agree.

The source was a beam of calcium coming off a tantalum oven, lit through a filter by a deuterium arc lamp, in a region about five millimetres high and three across. About seven in every hundred excited atoms came down in a way that put out two photons at once, one green and one violet. The detecting optics were the interesting part. To measure which way each photon was polarised they used piles of plates: ten sheets of glass three-tenths of a millimetre thick, set nearly at the angle at which glass reflects one polarisation and passes the other, mounted in hinged frames so that the whole stack could fold flat out of the beam. A Geneva mechanism, the sort of intermittent brass gear used in film projectors, clicked each stack round in steps of twenty-two and a half degrees.

The photomultipliers were cooled to hold their dark counts down, and even so they caught only about one photon in a thousand. With the polarisers folded out of the way the coincidence rate was three-tenths of a count per second at the start of a run, falling to one-tenth as the lamp dimmed through the night. So the apparatus counted in hundred-second blocks, alternating the polarisers in and out and stepping them round a set sequence, to average the drift away. It ran for about two hundred hours. The quantity they measured came out at fifty thousandths, give or take eight, where any theory of the kind Einstein wanted requires it to be zero or less. That is a little over six times the uncertainty. Clauser had expected the opposite result and had said so in writing beforehand.

Shimony had written to him in April 1969 that he put the odds at a million to one in favour of quantum mechanics and hoped he was wrong. Horne wrote the same week telling him to keep imagining it would come out against quantum theory, because that made it interesting. It did not come out that way. Clauser's own doctoral supervisor, Patrick Thaddeus, wrote reference letters warning departments not to hire him if it was for quantum mechanics experiments, on the grounds that the work was junk science. In August 1972 Shimony wrote to tell him that a department chairman at San Jose had written round asking whether what Clauser had been doing was real physics. Edwin Jaynes, whose own favourite theory Clauser's data had just undermined, wrote him a reference anyway. He never got a professorship.

Then Harvard got the other answer. Richard Holt, working under Francis Pipkin with mercury instead of calcium and calcite prisms instead of glass, counted for a hundred and fifty-four hours and got a number that agreed with Einstein and disagreed with quantum mechanics. They never published it. For three years the only two results in the world contradicted each other. Clauser rebuilt the mercury experiment himself, ran it for four hundred and twelve hours, and got quantum mechanics; Edward Fry at Texas, using a tunable dye laser to excite exactly the transition he wanted, got the same answer in eighty minutes. Clauser and Shimony later suggested a cause: stresses in the walls of the glass bulb had made the glass optically active and quietly turned the light. Harvard found the stresses and never re-ran. Holt said in 2005 that the source of the error remains unknown.

lessons.name: Have you a permanent position — Aspect's first meeting with Bell at CERN, switching the analysers while the photons are in flight, and the three experiments that followed
concepts: Alain Aspect was born at Agen in 1947, took a first doctorate on holography at Orsay, became disappointed with research, decided to be a schoolteacher instead, and came second in the national examination for teaching posts. He served his military obligation as civil service, teaching in Cameroon from 1971 to 1974. What turned him back was a new textbook he read out there, by Cohen-Tannoudji, Diu and Laloe. His previous studies in quantum physics, he said afterwards, had been totally disappointing, just solving equations about rigid rotators, not physics according to his view of physics, and the textbook changed his view entirely. He came home to a tenured post at his own former teachers' college, which left him free to choose what he worked on, and went to Orsay looking for a doctoral subject.

Christian Imbert handed him a bibliography on Bell's inequalities and told him to look into it for a possible subject. Aspect read the paper, saw that the two existing experiments disagreed with each other, and decided he wanted the one Bell had asked for in print, in which the settings are changed during the flight of the particles. Imbert told him to go to Geneva and discuss it with Bell first. He got an appointment without delay and turned up at Bell's office at CERN very impressed. While he explained his planned experiment, Bell listened in silence. Eventually Aspect stopped talking, and the first question came: have you a permanent position. Only after the answer was yes did Bell start talking about physics, encourage him, and warn him that most physicists considered all of this a subject for crackpots.

What made three experiments possible instead of one was the source. Where Berkeley had lit its calcium with an arc lamp and taken whatever came out, Aspect used two lasers tuned so that only atoms absorbing one photon from each would be lifted to the state he wanted: a krypton laser at four hundred and six nanometres and a tunable dye laser at five hundred and eighty-one, both focused to a spot fifty microns across, a few tens of milliwatts each, with two feedback loops holding the output steady to better than half a per cent for hours at a stretch. It gave about forty million cascades a second. Where Freedman and Clauser had needed two hundred hours to get one number, Aspect reached the same statistical accuracy in a hundred seconds.

The third experiment is the one Bell had asked for. Each photon, on its way out, met a switch that sent it down one of two paths to a different polariser, and the switch was flipping while the photon was in the air. The switches were built in the shop at Orsay and the working part of each one was water: two transducers driven in phase at twenty-five megahertz set up a standing wave of sound in it, and depending on where that wave stood at the instant the light arrived, the light went straight through or was bent aside. About a watt of sound. The switch flipped roughly every ten nanoseconds, and light took forty nanoseconds to cross from one switch to the other. The two sides ran off separate generators at different frequencies, so that nothing could coordinate them.

Aspect said in the paper itself that it was not conclusive, because the switching was quasiperiodic rather than truly random, and because the detectors caught so few of the pairs that you had to assume the ones you saw stood for the ones you missed. That assumption was the hole, and closing it took thirty-three years. In October 2015 a group at Delft ran the experiment on two electron spins in diamond at opposite ends of a campus, one and a third kilometres apart, arranged so that only trials announced in advance counted at all. In two hundred and twenty hours they got two hundred and forty-five usable trials, and every one of them was clean. Two more groups published in December, one of them working in the sub-basement of the Habsburg imperial palace in Vienna.

In 2018 a group set their analysers using the colour of light from quasars, emitted billions of years ago, on the argument that nothing could have arranged the settings in advance without reaching back nearly eight billion years to do it. The Nobel Prize in Physics was announced on the fourth of October 2022, to Aspect, Clauser and Anton Zeilinger, for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities. The affiliation the academy printed for Clauser is J. F. Clauser and Associates of Walnut Creek, California, which is his own consultancy, because he never held a university post. John Bell had died of a stroke on the first of October 1990, thirty-two years and three days before the announcement. He had been nominated. The prize is not given posthumously.

lessons.name: A concrete illustration of Bell inequalities — the CHSH game
concepts: Bell correlations can be explained through a game: two separated players each receive an independent uniformly random binary question and return a binary answer, without communicating after they receive their questions. They win when the XOR of their answers equals the AND of their questions. Any strategy using only local responses and shared advance information wins at most 75 percent on average; enumerating all 16 deterministic strategies proves the bound, and mixtures cannot improve it. Sharing an entangled quantum pair permits cos(pi/8)^2, about 85.36 percent, using appropriate measurements. This is an illustration of the quantum advantage, not guaranteed success, telepathy, instantaneous messages or a claim that Clauser ran a literal guessing game. The phrase a shared plan alone distinguishes ordinary prearranged local answers from an entangled resource, which also requires an agreed measurement strategy. Calculation and assumptions are saved in artifacts/hook-feedback-20260924/chsh-calculation.json. Introduce the game clearly before relating its limit to historical Bell tests.
